lessons.title: Handlers & the Fake res
lessons.explanation:
## Express mechanics, minus the server

An Express route handler is just a function of two arguments:

```js
function health(req, res) {
  res.status(200).json({ status: 'ok' });
}
```

`req` describes the incoming request; `res` is how you answer. In this course the grader has **no network and no Express** — so we simulate both, and the simulation is faithful enough that everything you write here is real Express muscle memory.

**The convention used by every exercise in this course:**

- `req` is a plain object: `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }` (exercises tell you which fields matter).
- `res` is a **recorder, constructed by the tests**:

```js
const res = {
  statusCode: 200,          // default, like Express
  body: undefined,
  status(c) { this.statusCode = c; return this; },
  json(b)   { this.body = b;       return this; },
};
health({ method: 'GET', path: '/health' }, res);
res.statusCode  // 200
res.body        // { status: 'ok' }
```

Walk through it: `status(c)` records the code **and returns `res`** — that return value is the whole trick behind the chain `res.status(201).json(...)`. `json(b)` records the body. After the handler runs, the test just inspects `res.statusCode` and `res.body`. Handlers return nothing; **responding IS the output**.

One more convention: a **204 No Content** response calls `res.status(204)` and never calls `json` — the body stays `undefined`.

### Common mistakes

- Returning data from a handler instead of calling `res.json`. Express ignores your return value; so do our tests.
- Forgetting that `res.json()` without `status()` means 200 — fine for success, wrong for errors.

## Everything, at once

This lesson is the final assembly: a `/todos` API with validation, auth, filtering, sorting, and pagination — built from the parts you now own. Todos look like `{ id, title, done, priority }` (id: number, done: boolean, priority: 1-5), and the store is a plain ARRAY the tests construct.

The query pipeline for `GET /todos` is worth staring at:

```js
// ?done=true&q=ship&sort=-priority&page=2&perPage=5
let result = todos;
result = filterTodos(result, query);       // done flag + q substring
result = sortTodos(result, query.sort);    // field, '-' prefix = desc
const page = paginate(result, p, pp);      // slice + meta
```

**Filter → sort → paginate, in that order.** Filtering first shrinks the work; sorting before pagination is *mandatory for correctness* — page 2 of a sorted list is meaningless unless the WHOLE list was sorted first. (This is also why databases do ORDER BY before LIMIT/OFFSET.)

Two more rules carried in from earlier lessons:

- Pure helpers do the data work; handlers do the HTTP work. You will build `filterTodos`/`sortTodos` as plain functions and then compose them inside handlers.
- Treat the inputs as hostile: every query param defaulted/clamped/whitelisted, every body validated with accumulated errors, every mutation behind the guards.

### Common mistakes

- Paginating before sorting (page contents change as data mutates — and differ from what any SQL implementation would return).
- Sorting the original array in place: `.sort()` MUTATES — copy first (`[...items].sort(...)`).
- Validating the body but forgetting to default optional fields (`done: false`) on create.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions: What is the signature of a basic Express-style route handler?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: Request first, response second, return value ignored — the handler *acts on* `res` rather than returning anything. Getting the argument order backwards is a rite of passage; the bugs it causes (calling `.json` on the request) at least fail loudly.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions: Why does `res.status(404).json({ ... })` work as a chain?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: `status(c) { this.statusCode = c; return this; }` — the `return this` is the entire mechanism, in our recorder and in real Express alike. Any method that returns its own object enables fluent chaining; you have met this before with string methods, where each call returns a new string.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions: A handler calls `res.json({ data: [] })` and never touches `status`. What status goes out?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: Both Express and our recorder start `statusCode` at 200, so plain `res.json(...)` is a 200 response. That default is why success paths look so terse — and why forgetting `status(400)` on an error path silently ships the error as a success.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions: In our simulation, a buggy handler calls `res.status(400).json(a)` and then later `res.status(200).json(b)`. What does the test observe?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: The recorder has no memory of "already sent" — later writes overwrite earlier ones, so the accidental 200 wins. (Real Express throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` on the second attempt — louder, but still a bug.) The fix is the same in both worlds: `return` after responding. The next lessons drill that habit.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions: Which values can `res.json(...)` meaningfully carry as a response body?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: `res.json(42)` or `res.json("ok")` are legal JSON documents. APIs still standardize on object envelopes (`{ data: ... }`) because objects can grow fields compatibly — a bare `42` response that later needs metadata becomes a breaking change. Legal ≠ advisable.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: The response a rate limiter sends when a client exceeds its budget (a later challenge has you build the limiter itself). Real ones add a Retry-After header; the envelope stays the standard shape regardless.
hints: One statement: chain status(...) and json(...).

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions:
Export `echoBody(req, res)` that responds `200` with `req.body` as the response body, exactly as received.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: Your first handler that READS the request. Echo endpoints look like toys but are real debugging tools (httpbin.org is a whole service of them) — when a client swears it sent something, an echo route settles it.
hints: The response body argument is just `req.body`.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions:
Export `whoCalled(req, res)` that responds `200` with `{ method, path }` taken from the request.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: Reading two request fields and shaping a response object — the minimal version of what every real handler does. The response is a NEW object; handlers should never hand pieces of `req` back by reference when they intend a snapshot.
hints: Build a fresh object from two req fields: `{ method: req.method, path: req.path }`.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions:
Export `greet(req, res)` that responds `200` with `{ message: 'Hello, <name>!' }` using `req.body.name`. When `req.body` is `null`/`undefined` or `req.body.name` is not a non-empty string, respond `400` with `{ error: { code: 'VALIDATION', message: 'name is required' } }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: The validate-then-respond shape in miniature: the guard clause handles every bad input in one place (optional chaining collapses "no body" and "no name" into the same undefined), responds 400, and — crucially — `return`s so the success line cannot also run. This early-return discipline is the fix for the double-respond bug from the quiz.
hints: Optional chaining `req.body?.name` survives a null body.
Validate first, respond 400 and RETURN, then the happy path below is unconditional.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions:
Export `noContent(req, res)` that responds `204` with NO body — call `res.status(204)` and never call `json`, so `res.body` stays `undefined`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: 204 means 'done, nothing to say' — sending ANY body with it is a protocol violation real servers will strip. In our convention the distinction is visible: `res.body` stays `undefined` because `json` was never called. You will use this for every successful DELETE.
hints: Just the status call. json(undefined) would record a body "event" — don't.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions: Per this course's convention, how does a handler produce a 204 No Content, and what will the tests see?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: A 204 carries no body by definition, so the honest simulation is to never call `json` — leaving `res.body` as `undefined` proves no body event happened. `{}` or `null` would both be bodies, and real servers strip bodies from 204s anyway.

Without `return`, execution falls straight through the `if` and the 200 overwrites the 400 — the exact failure mode from the earlier quiz, now fixed by you. `return res.status(...).json(...)` returns a value nobody reads, and that is fine: the return is for CONTROL FLOW, not data. This missing-return bug is, no exaggeration, one of the most common Express bugs in production code.
hints: After the 400 is recorded, does the function stop?
Add `return` before the error response (returning the res call expression is the idiomatic one-liner).

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions:
Export `makeStaticHandler(status, body)` — a FACTORY that returns a handler `(req, res)` which always responds with that status and body. `makeStaticHandler(503, { error: { code: 'MAINTENANCE', message: 'back soon' } })` gives a handler for maintenance mode.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: A closure: the returned handler remembers `status` and `body` from its creation. Factories-returning-handlers is the central pattern of this whole course — the next lessons use it to close over data stores and configuration. Note the third test: each call to the factory makes an independent handler; the closures do not interfere.
hints: Return an arrow function that closes over status and body.
The factory runs once; the returned handler runs per request.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions: In `makeStaticHandler(503, body)`, when does the factory run and when does the returned handler run?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: Two lifetimes: setup time (factories, configuration, store injection) and request time (handlers). Confusing them causes real bugs — expensive work accidentally placed in the handler runs on every request; per-request state accidentally placed in the factory is shared by all requests. Every `make...` in this course runs once; everything it returns runs per request.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: Each call to the factory creates a NEW `count` in a new closure: `a` counts 1, 2 while `b` starts over at 1. This independence is why tests can call `makeUserHandlers(new Map())` per test and never leak state between them — and why a shared store must be passed IN if sharing is what you want.
hints: Each factory call creates a fresh count variable.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions:
Export `echoRequestId(req, res)` — respond `200` with `{ requestId: <value of the 'x-request-id' header> }`, or `{ requestId: 'none' }` when the header (lowercase key in `req.headers`) is absent.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: Headers are the third input channel (after params and query), and `x-request-id` is the classic one: clients send it so that your logs and their logs can be correlated across the boundary. The `?? 'none'` keeps the response shape stable whether or not the client participated.
hints: Bracket access with the lowercase name, defaulted with `??`.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.instructions:
In the HTTP course you built pure functions returning `{ ok: true, ... }` / `{ ok: false, ... }` results. Bridge them to handlers.

Export `respondWith(res, result)` where `result` is either
- `{ ok: true, data }` → respond `200` with `{ data }`
- `{ ok: true, data, status }` → same but with that status (e.g. 201)
- `{ ok: false, status, code, message }` → respond with that status and `{ error: { code, message } }`

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/handler-b.explanation: This function is a seam: business logic stays pure (returns results, trivially unit-testable), and ONE adapter translates results into HTTP. Handlers shrink to `respondWith(res, doTheThing(req))`. Teams that build this seam get testable cores; teams that don't end up with business rules tangled into `res.status` calls everywhere. `?? 200` keeps the common success case terse while letting 201/204 override.
hints: Branch on result.ok.
Default the success status with `?? 200`.
The error branch re-shapes flat fields into the nested envelope.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions: Route pattern `/posts/:postId/comments`, actual request `GET /posts/10/comments?page=2`. What does the handler see?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Pattern captures land in `params`; query-string pairs land in `query` — two separate objects, and every value a string. The router fills `params`; the query parser fills `query`; the handler consumes both.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions: A user row has `id: 7` (a number). The handler does `users.find(u => u.id === req.params.id)` for the request `/users/7`. What happens?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: The silent killer of CRUD lesson one: `req.params.id` is the STRING '7', and strict equality against the number 7 is false, so `find` returns undefined and the handler 404s a user that exists. Either parse the param (`Number.parseInt`) or store string ids — but decide, and be consistent.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Everything out of a URL is a string: typeof says so, strict equality against a number fails, and `+ 1` concatenates to `'21'`. Only after `parseInt` does arithmetic behave. This four-line snippet is the whole lesson's thesis.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export `getUserId(req, res)` that responds `200` with `{ id: req.params.id }` — the captured param, still a string.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: A warmup to fix the mechanics: params live under `req.params`, keyed by the name after the `:` in the pattern. Notice the test passes `id: '42'` as a string — the router always does.
hints: One property read, one json call.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export `getSquare(req, res)`: parse `req.params.n` with `Number.parseInt(..., 10)`. If the result is `NaN`, respond `400` with `{ error: { code: 'BAD_REQUEST', message: 'n must be a number' } }`; otherwise respond `200` with `{ result: n * n }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: The worked example from the explanation, written by your own hands: parse with a radix, guard with `Number.isNaN` (the reliable check — remember `NaN === NaN` is false), 400-and-return on garbage. The validated number — and only it — flows into the logic.
hints: parse → Number.isNaN guard with 400 + return → compute.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export a factory `makeGetUser(users)` taking an ARRAY of user objects `{ id, name }` (string ids). It returns a handler that finds the user whose `id` equals `req.params.id`: found → `200` with `{ data: user }`; not found → `404` with `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'user <id> not found' } }` (interpolate the requested id).

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: The factory pattern meets data: `users` is injected at creation time (the tests construct it; a real app would pass a DB-backed store), so the handler itself stays a pure function of its inputs. String-vs-string comparison sidesteps the type trap from the quiz. The 404 message interpolates the id — specific errors cut debugging time on both sides of the API.
hints: The factory closes over `users`; the handler uses `.find` with a string comparison.
`find` returns undefined on a miss — that drives the 404 branch.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export `getLimit(req, res)`: read `req.query.limit`; default `10` when absent; parse with `Number.parseInt(..., 10)`; non-numeric or < 1 → `400` with `{ error: { code: 'BAD_REQUEST', message: 'limit must be a positive number' } }`; values over 50 are clamped to 50. Respond `200` with `{ limit: <number> }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Note the policy split: an ABSENT limit is fine (the API chooses a default), an INVALID limit is the client's error (400), and an oversized one is silently capped. Those three behaviors — default, reject, clamp — are deliberate design decisions you should be able to defend per-parameter. Clamping instead of rejecting large limits is kindness + self-protection in one move.
hints: Three distinct cases: absent (default), invalid (400), valid (clamp & respond).
Absent is `undefined` — handle it BEFORE parsing, since the default needs no validation.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export a factory `makeSearch(titles)` (an array of strings). The returned handler reads `req.query.q`: when missing or empty → `400` with `{ error: { code: 'BAD_REQUEST', message: 'q is required' } }`. Otherwise respond `200` with `{ data: matches }` where matches are the titles containing `q` case-insensitively (preserve original order and casing).

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Two API-design points hide in here. First: this endpoint REQUIRES its query param — defaults are not always right, and "search for nothing" is a client error. Second: an empty result set is a 200, not a 404 — the SEARCH succeeded; it found nothing. 404 is for "this route/resource does not exist", not "your query matched zero rows".
hints: Lowercase BOTH sides once; filter with includes.
Zero matches is a successful search — 200 with an empty array, never 404.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export a factory `makeTodoFilter(todos)` (array of `{ id, title, done }`). The handler reads `req.query.done`: absent → `200` with ALL todos in `{ data }`; `'true'` / `'false'` → only todos whose `done` matches; any other value → `400` with `{ error: { code: 'BAD_REQUEST', message: "done must be 'true' or 'false'" } }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: The three-state boolean from the HTTP course, now driving a handler: absent means "no filter", and the strict `'true'`/`'false'` whitelist keeps the contract crisp (silently treating `done=yes` as false would hide client bugs). `t.done === wanted` compares boolean to boolean — the string never touches the data.
hints: Three-way split: undefined / 'true' or 'false' / anything else.
Convert once: `const wanted = raw === 'true'` — then compare booleans to booleans.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions: The route is registered as `/users/:id`. A request arrives for `/users`. What happens?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: `/users/:id` has two segments; `/users` has one — no match, so the param handler is never consulted. Listing the collection needs its own route (`/users`). This is why CRUD registers list and get as two separate routes even though both are GETs on "users".

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Destructuring with defaults is a tidy first step for query handling: `page` was present so it keeps its value `'3'`, `perPage` was absent so the default `'20'` kicks in. But note the types — everything is STILL a string ('3', not 3); destructuring defaults replace the missing, they do not parse.
hints: Destructuring defaults fire only for undefined properties.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions: Export `toIntOr(raw, fallback)` — `Number.parseInt(raw, 10)`; return the fallback when the result is `NaN`. The workhorse for optional numeric query params.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Four lines that delete a dozen from every handler: `toIntOr(req.query.page, 1)` reads as intent. Note it deliberately does NOT clamp or floor — those are per-parameter policies layered on top; the helper does one job. (parseInt of undefined is NaN, so the missing case needs no special branch.)
hints: parseInt, then a ternary on Number.isNaN.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export `shoutWord(req, res)` for the route `/shout/:word` — respond `200` with `{ shout: '<WORD>!' }`: the param uppercased with `'!'` appended.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Not every param needs a 400 branch: a string param used AS a string has no invalid values, so transform-and-respond is the whole handler. Validation effort should track what the value must BE — numbers, ids, and enums earn guards; free text often does not.
hints: Read the param, transform, respond — no validation needed since any string uppercases.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export `echoInputs(req, res)` responding `200` with `{ params: req.params, query: req.query }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: A debugging endpoint that makes the two input channels visible side by side. When a route mysteriously misbehaves, temporarily pointing it at an echo like this answers "what did the router actually give me?" in one request.
hints: Two fields into one response object.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export `greetQuery(req, res)` that reads `req.query.name`; absent or empty → use `'world'`. Respond `200` with `{ message: 'Hello, <name>!' }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: For once truthiness (`||`) beats `??`: the spec says empty string should ALSO default, and `'' || 'world'` delivers exactly that. Choosing between || and ?? is a per-field decision about whether empty-but-present counts as provided.
hints: `req.query.name || 'world'` — here || is RIGHT because empty string should also fall back.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export `getSorted(req, res)` that reads `req.query.sort`; absent → default `'name'`; must be `'name'` or `'date'`, anything else → `400` with `{ error: { code: 'BAD_REQUEST', message: "sort must be 'name' or 'date'" } }`. Respond `200` with `{ sort: <value> }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Sort values eventually reach a database ORDER BY — the whitelist is what stands between `?sort=` and SQL injection. Enum query params should always be validated against an explicit list, and the test's hostile value shows why.
hints: Default with ??, then validate against the two allowed strings.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export `getStatusReport(req, res)` that reads `req.query.verbose`: exactly `'true'` → respond `200` with `{ status: 'ok', uptime: 'long', memory: 'fine' }`; ANY other value or absent → `200` with just `{ status: 'ok' }` (flags are lenient — no 400s).

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Contrast with the strict done-filter earlier: a FILTER changes which data you get (wrong value = wrong answer = 400), while a cosmetic FLAG only changes presentation, so silently ignoring junk is friendlier than failing. Strictness should track the cost of misunderstanding.
hints: One strict comparison against 'true'; everything else takes the terse path.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Handlers stay slim when query parsing is its own function. Export `parseListQuery(query)` taking the raw query object (all strings, possibly missing) and returning `{ page, perPage, q }`:
- `page`: parseInt, default 1, floor 1 (NaN or < 1 → 1)
- `perPage`: parseInt, default 20, floor 1, cap 100
- `q`: the trimmed string, or `null` when absent or empty after trimming
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Pulling parsing out of the handler pays twice: the handler reads like a sentence (`const opts = parseListQuery(req.query)`), and this function is testable without any fake res at all — it is just data in, data out. Notice it never throws and never responds; policy (what to do about bad values) was decided here as defaults, so the handler has no error path for the query at all.
hints: Same pagination gauntlet as the HTTP course, plus a trimmed q.
Whitespace-only q becomes null — trim first, then test for empty.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions: Export `clampInt(n, min, max)` returning `n` forced into the inclusive range — below min → min, above max → max, otherwise unchanged.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: The clamp from the fundamentals course, back in its natural habitat: `clampInt(toIntOr(req.query.perPage, 20), 1, 100)` is the entire perPage policy in one readable line. Small pure helpers composing into policies is the texture of good handler code.
hints: Math.max enforces the floor, Math.min the ceiling.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: A pattern like `/range/:from/:to` produces MULTIPLE captures in one params object. Each is independently a string, each gets its own parse — and once parsed, real comparisons and arithmetic work (`3 < 5`, `5 - 3`). Cross-field validation (from ≤ to) is the handler's next job.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export `getRange(req, res)` for the route `/range/:from/:to`:
- parse both params with `Number.parseInt(..., 10)`; either NaN → `400` `{ error: { code: 'BAD_REQUEST', message: 'from and to must be numbers' } }`
- `from > to` → `400` `{ error: { code: 'BAD_REQUEST', message: 'from must not exceed to' } }`
- otherwise `200` with `{ data: [from, ..., to] }` — the inclusive integer range.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Cross-field validation has a natural ordering: individual validity first (both parse), then the relationship (from ≤ to) — you cannot meaningfully compare a NaN. Distinct messages per failure mode tell the client exactly which rule bit. Date ranges, price ranges, and page spans all follow this two-tier shape.
hints: Parse both, reject NaN together, THEN compare them.
Cross-field checks can only run after both fields individually parsed.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions: `GET /users?role=sysadmin` matches zero users (the role exists; nobody has it). Correct response?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: A filtered LIST that matches nothing succeeded at its job. 404 belongs to routes/resources that do not exist (`/users/999`), not to empty query results — clients treat 404 as "retry pointless / show error", which is wrong for an empty table. (204 is for responses that deliberately carry no body at all, like DELETE.)

bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.instructions:
Export a factory `makeListItems(items)`. The returned handler supports `?page` and `?perPage`:
- parse with the usual rules — page default 1 (floor 1), perPage default 20 (floor 1, cap 100), non-numeric → the default
- respond `200` with `{ data, meta: { page, perPage, total, totalPages } }` where data is the correct slice (page 1 = first `perPage` items) and `totalPages = Math.ceil(total / perPage)`.
A page past the end returns empty `data` with correct meta.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/route-par.explanation: Everything in one place: the factory closes over the data, the query gauntlet normalizes input (note that here even garbage never 400s — list endpoints conventionally degrade to defaults), and the response carries the full pagination envelope. This handler, with a database call swapped in for `items.slice`, IS the list endpoint of production APIs.
hints: This is parseListQuery + paginatedResponse from earlier courses, fused into one handler.
Parse/default/clamp first; the slice math is `(page - 1) * perPage`.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: A valid `POST /users` inserts a row. The conventional response?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: The client needs the server-assigned id to do anything further with the resource, so 201 + the created object is the contract. Returning the whole list wastes bandwidth and leaks other rows; 204 would force an immediate follow-up GET just to learn the id.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: `DELETE /users/9` returned 204. The client, retrying on a flaky network, sends the exact same DELETE again. What should the second response be, and is this a problem?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: From the HTTP course: idempotency is about state, not responses. The second DELETE finds nothing → 404 is the truthful answer, and user 9 is equally gone. (Some APIs return 204 for both to simplify clients — a defensible choice — but 404 is not a bug.)

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: Why do our CRUD handlers come from a factory (`makeUserHandlers(store)`) instead of importing a shared top-level `store`?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: A module-level store is global mutable state: tests would leak data into each other and run-order would matter. Injecting the store makes every dependency visible in the signature — swap a Map for a real repository object with the same methods and the handlers never know. This is dependency injection with zero framework.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: Every CRUD test in this lesson builds a FRESH store (`new Map([...])`) rather than sharing one across tests. What does that buy?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: A shared store makes test ORDER part of the test: delete-test runs before get-test and suddenly get-test fails, or worse, passes only because an earlier test seeded data. Fresh fixtures per test are the testing twin of the dependency-injection quiz — the same factory design enables both.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: The whole Map API a CRUD store needs: `get` (undefined on miss), `has`, `set`, `delete` — which returns `true` the first time and `false` when there was nothing to delete (that boolean will drive your 404 branch) — and `[...store.values()]` to materialize the list.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: Export `nextId(ids)` — given an array of existing string ids (decimal numbers), return the next id as a STRING: one more than the numeric maximum, `'1'` for an empty array. `['1', '3']` → `'4'` (NOT `'3'` — size-based schemes collide after deletions).
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: The `['1', '3']` case is the whole argument: length-plus-one would mint '3' and silently overwrite an existing row. Max-plus-one never reuses an id, which also matters beyond collisions — reused ids resurrect stale links, caches, and permissions pointing at the dead row. Note `'10'` vs `'9'`: NUMERIC max (10), not string max ('9' > '10' lexicographically!).
hints: Track the numeric max over the array, then String(max + 1).
Why not length + 1? Delete id 2 from [1,2,3] and create — boom.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Export `makeList(store)` (a Map of id → object). The handler responds `200` with `{ data: [...store.values()] }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: `store.values()` is an iterator, not an array — spreading materializes it into something `json` can carry. The third test makes the closure's nature visible: the handler holds a reference to the LIVE store, so data added after the factory ran still shows up. That liveness is exactly what you want from an injected dependency.
hints: Spread store.values() into an array; Maps are not JSON-serializable directly.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Export `makeGet(store)`. The handler looks up `req.params.id` with `store.get`: found → `200` with `{ data: user }`; missing → `404` with `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'user <id> not found' } }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: The guard-respond-return triplet, now against a store. `Map.get` returning `undefined` (instead of throwing) maps perfectly onto the 404 branch. Every read-one endpoint in existence is this function with a fancier store.
hints: store.get returns undefined on a miss — guard, 404, return.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Export `makeCreate(store)`. The handler:
1. Validates `req.body.name` is a non-empty string → otherwise `400` with `{ error: { code: 'VALIDATION', message: 'name is required' } }` and the store untouched.
2. Generates the id: String(numeric max of existing keys + 1), `'1'` for an empty store.
3. Inserts `{ id, name }` into the store and responds `201` with `{ data: <the new user> }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: The full create choreography: validate (and bail before any mutation — test 4 checks the store stayed clean), mint a collision-proof id, insert, respond 201 with the stored object. Responding with the SAME object you stored guarantees the client sees exactly what persistence saw — divergence there is a classic source of "it looked saved" bugs.
hints: Validate FIRST — a 400 must leave no trace in the store.
The id scan is the nextId logic over store.keys().
Build the user object once; set it AND send it.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Export `makeUpdate(store)`. The handler:
- Missing id → `404` with `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'user <id> not found' } }`.
- Otherwise merge ONLY the fields `name` and `email` from `req.body` (each only when not `undefined`) into the existing user, store the merged object, and respond `200` with `{ data: merged }`. Other body fields (like `id` or `isAdmin`) must be ignored.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: PATCH = merge, and the merge is an ALLOW-LIST: only `name` and `email` may change, so the hostile body in test 3 (`id: '999', isAdmin: true`) bounces off — the mass-assignment defense from the validation lesson, now in a handler. The `!== undefined` checks make "field omitted" mean "leave it alone", which is the entire semantic difference between PATCH and PUT.
hints: Copy the existing user with spread, then conditionally overwrite the two allowed fields.
`Object.assign(existing, req.body)` is the vulnerable version — the allow-list is the point.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Export `makeRemove(store)`. The handler deletes `req.params.id` from the store: existed → `204` with no body (never call `json`); did not exist → `404` with `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'user <id> not found' } }`. Hint: `store.delete` returns a boolean.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: `Map.delete` returning its success boolean lets one call serve as both the mutation and the existence check — no get-then-delete race. The second test replays the delete and expects 404, codifying the idempotency discussion: same state, truthful response. And per the convention, 204 leaves `res.body` untouched.
hints: `store.delete` both mutates and reports — one call drives both branches.
The 204 branch must not call json.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: In handler terms, what separates a PUT update from a PATCH update of `/users/1`?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: The method is a promise about omitted fields: PUT says "this body is the complete new truth" (so an omitted email DELETES the email); PATCH says "change only what I mention". A handler that merges on PUT or replaces on PATCH is lying to its clients in a way tests rarely catch but integrations always do.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: Spread order tells the story: the PATCH shape starts from `existing` so the omitted email survives (`a@x.io`); the PUT shape starts from scratch (only the id is preserved by policy) so the omitted email is `undefined`. Both agree on the field that WAS sent. This is the quiz above, executable.
hints: Which construction keeps fields the body omitted?

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Export `makeReplace(store)` implementing PUT semantics:
- `req.body.name` must be a non-empty string → else `400` with `{ error: { code: 'VALIDATION', message: 'name is required' } }`
- missing id → `404` with `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'user <id> not found' } }`
- otherwise the stored object becomes EXACTLY `{ id, name }` plus `email` ONLY if the body provided one — fields the body omits are dropped (that is what PUT means). Respond `200` with `{ data }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: Side by side with `makeUpdate`, the single structural difference is where the object starts: `{ ...existing }` (PATCH) versus `{ id, name }` built fresh (PUT) — and test 1 proves the consequence: the old email vanishes because the body omitted it. The id always comes from the URL; honoring a body-supplied id would let clients overwrite arbitrary rows.
hints: Contrast with makeUpdate: build the new object from the BODY, not from the existing record.
The id comes from the URL, never the body — keep it authoritative.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Export `makeCount(store)` — the handler responds `200` with `{ count: store.size }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: Aggregates (counts, sums, stats) get their own read-only endpoints rather than forcing clients to fetch everything and count locally. `store.size` is the Map version of `SELECT COUNT(*)` — O(1) here, and the shape of the endpoint is identical when a database does the counting.
hints: Map tracks its own size.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Export `makeExists(store)` — the handler checks `req.params.id`: present in the store → `200` with `{ exists: true }`; absent → `404` with `{ exists: false }` (note: NOT the error envelope — this endpoint's contract is the boolean itself, in both cases).

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: `has` instead of `get` signals intent: existence, not content. The status still tells the truth (404 for absent) while the body carries the answer in both cases — the HTTP-level signal for machines-in-the-middle, the body for the application. Real APIs often expose this as a HEAD request on the item route, where only the status survives.
hints: `store.has` — no need to fetch the value you will not send.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Export `makeCreateUnique(store)` — like create, plus a conflict check. Users are `{ id, name, email }`; `req.body` must have non-empty string `name` and `email` (→ `400`, `{ error: { code: 'VALIDATION', message: 'name and email are required' } }`). If any existing user already has the same email → `409` with `{ error: { code: 'CONFLICT', message: "email '<email>' is already taken" } }` and no insert. Otherwise insert with the max+1 id rule and respond `201` with `{ data: user }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: The check order mirrors the status-code ladder from the HTTP course: malformed input (400) is judged before business-state conflicts (409), and only a fully-approved request mutates. In a real database this scan is a UNIQUE index and the 409 comes from catching its violation — but the handler shape, and the promise that failed requests leave no trace, are identical.
hints: Order: validate (400) → scan for conflict (409) → insert (201).
Loop store.values() for the email check.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: Why is a `Map` a slightly better in-memory store than a plain object (`{}`) keyed by id?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: A plain object works until an id collides with something on Object.prototype (`'constructor'`, `'__proto__'` — real ids in real incidents) or you need size (Object.keys(o).length every time). Map was designed as a dictionary; objects were drafted into the job. For serialization Maps need the `[...map.values()]` step you have been writing — the one Map inconvenience.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: The collision scenario executed: after deleting '2', size-based minting proposes '3' — and `store.has('3')` is `true`, meaning a create would OVERWRITE user 3. Max-based minting proposes '4', safely fresh. One printed `true` is the entire argument for nextId.
hints: After the delete: size is 2, but which ids exist?

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: Export `sortIds(ids)` returning a NEW array of the string ids sorted by their NUMERIC value: `['10', '2', '1']` → `['1', '2', '10']` (default `.sort()` would give `['1', '10', '2']`!). Do not mutate the input.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: Two classic traps in one line: `.sort()` with no comparator sorts LEXICOGRAPHICALLY ('10' < '2' because '1' < '2'), and it mutates in place. The spread-copy plus numeric comparator fixes both. Any store listing that should read 1, 2, ..., 10 instead of 1, 10, 2 needs this.
hints: Copy first (sort mutates!), compare with Number(a) - Number(b).

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Export `makeGetWithFields(store)` — like a normal get (404 with the usual `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'user <id> not found' } }`), but supporting `?fields=name,email`:
- no `fields` query param → `200` with `{ data: user }` (everything)
- `fields` present → split on `','` and respond with ONLY those properties of the user that exist (unknown names silently skipped; `id` is NOT automatically included).

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: Sparse fieldsets (`?fields=`) let bandwidth-conscious clients request only what they render — a standard REST refinement (JSON:API specifies exactly this parameter). The implementation is your `pickFields` allow-list walking client-chosen names, with `in` guarding against manufacturing undefined keys. Note the 404 still fires first: existence questions precede shaping questions.
hints: 404 first, then branch on whether fields was provided.
The picking loop is pickFields from the HTTP course, fed by split(',').

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: Our conflict check scans every user for a matching email. For a real system with a million users, what replaces the scan?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: The scan has a deeper flaw than speed: two simultaneous requests can BOTH pass the check, then both insert (a race condition — check-then-act is not atomic). A database UNIQUE constraint makes the insert itself the check, atomically. The handler pattern survives: attempt, catch the constraint violation, 409.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions: After a create or update, the handler responds with the object it just STORED (not the raw request body). Why does the distinction matter?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: Between body and store sit the id generator, defaults, trimming, and the allow-list — the stored record is the TRUTH, and the response should be a receipt for it. Echoing the body instead hides every one of those transformations and produces "but it showed me X!" bugs when the next GET returns Y.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.instructions:
Assemble everything. Export `makeUserHandlers(store)` returning `{ list, get, create, update, remove }` with exactly the behaviors drilled above:
- `list`: 200 `{ data: [...store.values()] }`
- `get`: 200 `{ data }` / 404 `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'user <id> not found' } }`
- `create`: body needs non-empty string `name` → else 400 `{ error: { code: 'VALIDATION', message: 'name is required' } }`; insert `{ id, name }` with max+1 id; 201 `{ data }`
- `update`: 404 like get; else merge allowed fields `name`/`email` (when not undefined), store, 200 `{ data }`
- `remove`: 404 like get; else delete, 204, no body

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/crud-hand.explanation: The capstone of the module: five handlers over one injected store, with the shared 404 pulled into a local helper (the factory's closure is a natural private scope for it). The lifecycle test exercises the handlers AS A SYSTEM — create feeds get feeds update feeds remove — which is exactly how an integration test for a real Express router reads. Swap the Map for a repository backed by SQL and this factory ships.
hints: You have written all five bodies already — assemble them into one returned object.
A shared `notFound(res, id)` helper inside the factory removes the triplicated 404.
All five handlers close over the SAME store, so the lifecycle test flows through it.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Error codes in this course are SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE tokens ('NOT_FOUND', 'RATE_LIMITED'). What property matters most about them?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: The casing is just convention (loud, visibly-a-constant); the CONTRACT is what counts: each code is a promise to every client that wrote `if (error.code === 'CONFLICT')`. Treat the code list like a public enum — append-only, documented, reviewed. Messages can be reworded freely precisely because codes cannot.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: An unexpected exception (`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')`) escapes a handler. What belongs in the 500 response body?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: Unexpected error messages leak implementation detail (table names, file paths, library versions) that helps attackers and confuses users. The client learns 'our fault, not yours'; the stack trace goes to logging where YOU can see it. Expected errors (400, 404...) carry real messages because you wrote those messages for clients on purpose.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: In real Express 4, a SYNCHRONOUS throw inside a handler with no error middleware configured results in...
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: Express wraps synchronous handler calls in try/catch and routes throws to error-handling middleware — the built-in one sends a 500. (The historical trap was ASYNC throws: before Express 5, a rejected promise with no .catch skipped this safety net entirely and could crash the process.) Our simulated wrapper plays the role of that safety net.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Why tag errors with a `name` like `'NotFoundError'` instead of the handler choosing a status number at the throw site?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: A service function that throws `NotFoundError` can be reused from a CLI, a queue worker, or a test — none of which know what a 404 is. The HTTP layer owns the translation, in exactly one place. If the team later decides validation failures should be 422 instead of 400, that is a one-line change.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: An `Error` carries two useful strings: `message` (human detail) and `name` (its KIND — reassignable, and the conventional way to tag error types without classes). Throwing and catching preserves the object identity, so the catch block can branch on `caught.name`. That branch is what the wrapper below automates.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Export `statusForError(name)` mapping: `'ValidationError'` → 400, `'AuthError'` → 401, `'ForbiddenError'` → 403, `'NotFoundError'` → 404, `'ConflictError'` → 409, anything else → 500.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: Note what maps to 500: `TypeError`, plain `Error` — the errors NOBODY expected. The table enumerates the errors your domain deliberately throws; everything else is by definition a bug, and 500 is the honest status for bugs. The `??` fallback encodes "unknown = our fault".
hints: Lookup object with ?? 500 — the shape you used for pickStatus.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions:
Export `toHttpError(err)` where `err` is `{ name, message }`. Return `{ status, body }`:
- Known names map as before, with codes: ValidationError→400 `'VALIDATION'`, AuthError→401 `'UNAUTHORIZED'`, ForbiddenError→403 `'FORBIDDEN'`, NotFoundError→404 `'NOT_FOUND'`, ConflictError→409 `'CONFLICT'` — and the body keeps `err.message`.
- Any other name → `{ status: 500, body: { error: { code: 'INTERNAL', message: 'internal server error' } } }` — the original message is NOT leaked.
Body shape: `{ error: { code, message } }`.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: The security property lives in the asymmetry: known errors carry messages you authored for clients; the unknown branch substitutes a fixed string because `err.message` of a bug can contain anything (the TypeError case would have leaked code structure). This one function is the single source of truth for your API's error contract.
hints: A table of { status, code } per name; the miss branch builds the fixed 500.
Only KNOWN errors keep their message — check the TypeError case.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: What is the strongest argument for ONE shared error wrapper over a try/catch inside each handler?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: With per-handler catches, every handler is an opportunity to format an error differently, leak a message, or forget a case — and code review is the only defense. With one wrapper, divergence is impossible by construction. (Per-handler try/catch still has a place: when a handler can meaningfully RECOVER, not just translate.)

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: The catch block is the whole policy in two lines: known names surface their message (`NotFoundError went wrong`), unknown ones get the fixed string. Running both kinds through the same catch shows the asymmetry side by side — exactly what your wrapper does per request.
hints: Which of the two names is in the known list?

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Export `isClientFault(name)` → `true` when the error name maps to a 4xx in our table (ValidationError, AuthError, ForbiddenError, NotFoundError, ConflictError) and `false` for anything else (which maps to 500 — our fault).
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: The known/unknown split from toHttpError, reduced to its essence: every error we deliberately throw blames the request (4xx); every error we did not anticipate blames us (500). Monitoring dashboards use this exact predicate — 4xx volume is "clients being clients", 5xx volume pages someone.
hints: Membership in the known-error list IS the 4xx predicate.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Export `shouldAlert(name)` — the inverse policy: `true` only for error names NOT in the known table (unknown errors are bugs worth waking someone for); the five known names → `false`.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: A thousand 404s before lunch is Tuesday; one TypeError is a defect. Alerting on expected errors trains the team to ignore alerts (the real cost of false positives), so the policy inverts the known-list: only the unexpected pages anyone. Note how having ONE table of known errors lets three different functions (status, fault, alert) stay consistent.
hints: One ! in front of the membership check.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Export `errorLogLine(err, req)` where `err` is `{ name, message }` and `req` is `{ method, path }`. Return `'<name> on <METHOD> <path>: <message>'` — e.g. `'NotFoundError on GET /users/9: user 9 not found'`.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: The message the CLIENT must not see (for 500s) is exactly what the LOG must capture — alongside which request triggered it, or you will be reproducing from guesswork. This line is what the catch block of a production wrapper writes before sending the sanitized response.
hints: One template literal, four interpolations.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions:
Export two helpers that BUILD tagged errors (without throwing):
- `notFoundError(resource, id)` → an `Error` with `name = 'NotFoundError'` and message `'<resource> <id> not found'`
- `validationError(message)` → an `Error` with `name = 'ValidationError'` and that message
Both must return real `Error` instances (`instanceof Error`).
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: Real `Error` instances matter: they capture stack traces for your logs, and `instanceof Error` checks in catch-all code keep working. Setting `.name` is the lightweight alternative to subclassing (`class NotFoundError extends Error` is the heavyweight version — same effect). Returning rather than throwing lets the CALLER decide: `throw notFoundError('users', id)` reads like a sentence.
hints: new Error(message), then overwrite .name, then return (not throw).

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions:
Export `sendValidationErrors(res, errors)` where `errors` is an array of `{ field, message }`. Respond `400` with `{ error: { code: 'VALIDATION', message: 'validation failed', details: errors } }` — the standard envelope plus a `details` array for the field-level specifics.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: The envelope is extensible by design: `code` and `message` stay for generic clients, while `details` gives forms the per-field array your `validateBody` produces. Clients that do not know about `details` ignore it — additive evolution, no breakage. This marries the validation lesson to the error lesson.
hints: The envelope grows a third key, details, INSIDE error.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions:
Export `withErrorHandling(handler)` returning a new handler that calls `handler(req, res)` inside try/catch. On a throw, translate with the toHttpError table (same codes/statuses as before — ValidationError/400/VALIDATION, AuthError/401/UNAUTHORIZED, ForbiddenError/403/FORBIDDEN, NotFoundError/404/NOT_FOUND, ConflictError/409/CONFLICT, anything else → 500 with code 'INTERNAL' and the fixed message 'internal server error') and respond accordingly. Non-throwing handlers behave exactly as before.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: The payoff of the whole lesson: handlers wrapped in this can simply `throw notFoundError('users', id)` from any depth and the correct, consistent response happens. One wrapper replaces a try/catch in every handler (and this is literally what Express error middleware does — one function, mounted once). Test 4 proves the leak-protection: the TypeError's "secret internal detail" never reaches the client.
hints: A factory again: return a (req, res) arrow that try/catches the wrapped call.
The catch block is your toHttpError logic, responding instead of returning.
Make sure the unknown branch sends the FIXED message, not err.message.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions:
Now write a handler designed to live INSIDE the wrapper. Export `makeGetOrThrow(store)` (Map of id → user). The returned handler:
- found → `200` with `{ data: user }`
- missing → **throw** an `Error` with `name = 'NotFoundError'` and message `'user <id> not found'` — do NOT touch res in that case.
(The tests call it both directly — expecting the throw — and through a catch wrapper.)

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: Compare this to `makeGet` from the CRUD lesson: the logic is identical, but the error PATH is now a throw instead of a `res` call — which means this handler no longer knows or cares that 404 exists. Pair it with `withErrorHandling` and the behavior matches `makeGet` exactly, with the HTTP knowledge living in one shared place. The test checks `res` stayed untouched on the throw path: throwing AND responding would be the double-respond bug in new clothes.
hints: The 404 branch becomes: build the tagged error, throw it, done.
Throwing exits the function — no return needed after it.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Our wrapper try/catches a SYNCHRONOUS handler call. What breaks when handlers become async (`async (req, res) => { ... }`)?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: A sync try/catch only catches what throws DURING the call — an async handler returns its promise instantly and fails later. The async wrapper is `async (req, res) => { try { await handler(req, res); } catch ... }`. This exact gap was THE classic Express 4 footgun (rejected promises skipping error middleware); Express 5 finally awaits handlers natively.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Export `httpError(status, code, message)` returning `{ status, body: { error: { code, message } } }` — the little constructor every error path can share.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: With this constructor, `toHttpError` collapses to table lookups feeding one builder, and no code anywhere hand-assembles the envelope — the nesting exists in exactly one line of the codebase. When a `details` field joins the envelope someday, one function changes.
hints: Three arguments nested into the standard shape.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Export `getOrThrow(store, id, resource)` — NOT a handler, a store helper: return `store.get(id)` when present; otherwise THROW an `Error` with `name = 'NotFoundError'` and message `'<resource> <id> not found'`. Handlers inside the wrapper then write `const user = getOrThrow(store, req.params.id, 'user')` and simply proceed.
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: The throwing style pays off at the DATA layer: every lookup in every handler becomes one line with no 404 branch, because the branch lives here and the translation lives in the wrapper. `const user = getOrThrow(...); const post = getOrThrow(...)` — two lookups, zero error plumbing, both correctly 404 on miss. This is the pattern ORMs encourage with methods like findOrFail.
hints: Get, check undefined, throw the tagged error, else return.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions:
CRUD factories return OBJECTS of handlers — wrap them all at once. Export `wrapAll(handlers)` taking an object whose values are handler functions and returning a NEW object with the same keys where every handler is wrapped in the standard try/catch translation (same table and 500 behavior as withErrorHandling). The original object must not be modified.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object `{ method, path, params, query, body, headers }`; `res` is a recorder the tests provide — `statusCode` starts at 200, `body` starts undefined, and `status(code)` / `json(body)` each record their argument and return `res` so calls chain.)*
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: Transforming every value of an object through a function is a pattern worth owning (lodash calls it mapValues), and here it operationalizes the "everything is mounted wrapped" discipline: `wrapAll(makeUserHandlers(store))` makes it impossible for one route to forget its safety net. The identity test (`wrapped.a !== original.a`) is how you verify wrapping actually happened.
hints: Write (or reuse) a single-handler wrap function, then map it over Object.entries.
Build a fresh output object — do not assign onto the input.

bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.instructions: Using the wrapper approach, which statement about a new `createOrder` handler is true?
bootforge/express-api/handlers/error-res.explanation: That is the contract the wrapper buys you: handlers speak in domain errors, the wrapper speaks HTTP, and the mounting site (`withErrorHandling(createOrder)`) is where they meet. The discipline to maintain is simply that everything is mounted wrapped — which real apps guarantee by wrapping inside their route-registration helper.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: What distinguishes a middleware from a handler, mechanically?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Same `req`/`res`, plus the baton: `(req, res, next)`. A middleware is a gatekeeper-or-decorator that usually passes control on; a handler terminates the pipeline by responding. (In Express they are literally the same function type — the handler just never uses its third argument.)

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: A middleware runs its logic and then neither responds nor calls `next()`. In real Express, the client experiences...
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Express does not time out requests on its own: with the baton dropped, no later middleware runs and no response is written — the socket just stays open. These bugs are maddening because nothing ERRORS; things merely never finish. Our runChain simulation models it as "chain stops, res untouched".

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Chain A: `[auth, logger]`. Chain B: `[logger, auth]`. A request with a bad token arrives. What differs?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Short-circuiting means everything AFTER the rejecting middleware is skipped — including the logger in chain A. Since failed auth attempts are precisely the traffic you want visibility into, loggers conventionally go first. The array order is a real design decision, reviewed like code.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: mw1 passes the baton, mw2 drops it, so the loop breaks before mw3 — the trace reads `mw1 -> mw2`. Neither mw3 nor the handler ever ran (the handler isn't even in the loop here). Seeing the short-circuit as a plain loop-and-break demystifies the whole mechanism.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: A buggy middleware calls `next()` in BOTH branches of an if/else AND falls through to a final unconditional `next()`. In real Express, calling next twice causes...
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Each `next()` resumes the pipeline from this middleware's successor — twice means everything downstream executes twice, and the second response attempt explodes. The fix is the discipline you have been practicing since the handlers lesson: `return next()` or early-return after responding, so exactly one exit executes.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: A complete test for a GATEKEEPER middleware (like requireBody) asserts... (pick the fullest correct set)
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The middleware contract is respond-XOR-next, so each branch needs BOTH assertions: a middleware that responds 400 and then also calls next passes any status-only test while corrupting the pipeline. Every gatekeeper test in this course asserts the negative space (`called === false`, `res.body === undefined`) for exactly this reason.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `makeLogger(log)` — a factory taking an ARRAY. The returned middleware pushes `'<METHOD> <path>'` onto that array and calls `next()`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The purest middleware personality: pure observation. It decorates nothing and blocks nothing — push, next, done. Injecting the log array (instead of console.log) is what makes it testable; a real logger injected the same way could write anywhere.
hints: Push the formatted string, then next() — observe-and-pass, never respond.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `requireBody(req, res, next)` — when `req.body` is `null` or `undefined`, respond `400` with `{ error: { code: 'BAD_REQUEST', message: 'body required' } }` and do NOT call next. Otherwise call `next()` and leave res alone.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The gatekeeper personality: one check, two mutually exclusive exits. The tests pin BOTH sides of the contract — the reject path must respond AND withhold next; the pass path must call next AND not respond. Every protective middleware you write will be this shape with a different predicate.
hints: Respond-or-next, never both. `return` after the 400 enforces it.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `makeRequestId(state)` where `state` is `{ last: 0 }`. The returned middleware increments `state.last`, assigns the new value to `req.id`, and calls `next()`. Each request gets a unique, increasing id.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The decorator personality: enrich `req` so everything downstream gets the data for free — handlers can log `req.id`, return it in error responses, and correlate a user bug report with the exact server log line. Real systems use the same pattern with UUIDs and call it a correlation id.
hints: Mutate the shared state, decorate req, pass on.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `blockMethods(blocked)` — factory over an array of method names. The middleware: when `req.method` is in the list, respond `405` with `{ error: { code: 'METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED', message: '<METHOD> is not allowed' } }`; otherwise `next()`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Configuration-by-closure: the factory captures WHICH methods to block, so one implementation serves any policy (`blockMethods(['TRACE'])` is a real hardening move — TRACE echoes requests and has been used in attacks). 405 with the offending method named keeps the error self-explanatory.
hints: Gatekeeper shape again; the factory bakes in the blocklist.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `requireJson(req, res, next)`: for body-carrying methods (POST, PUT, PATCH), the `content-type` header (lowercase key in `req.headers`) must START WITH `'application/json'` — otherwise respond `415` with `{ error: { code: 'UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE', message: 'content-type must be application/json' } }`. Other methods (GET, DELETE, ...) always pass. Valid requests → `next()`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: HTTP-course knowledge operationalized: `startsWith` (not `===`) tolerates the charset parameter, 415 is the precise "right endpoint, wrong body format" status, and the method gate keeps bodiless requests out of the check entirely. Mounted once, this guarantees every handler downstream can assume parsed JSON.
hints: Two nested conditions: body-carrying method, then the startsWith check from the HTTP course.
GET/DELETE must pass unconditionally — they carry no body to type-check.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Which split of middleware between GLOBAL (every request) and PER-ROUTE is conventional?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The dividing question is "does the policy vary by endpoint?" Observability and hygiene apply uniformly → global. WHO may do WHAT is inherently per-endpoint (public /health, authenticated /me, admin-only /users DELETE) → attached per route. Making a per-route concern global either locks everyone out or protects nothing.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Logger, auth, request-id stamper, rate limiter — which are DECORATORS (enrich req, always pass) and which are GATEKEEPERS (may short-circuit)?
