bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Classifying a middleware by its exits clarifies its tests: a decorator/observer must ALWAYS call next and never touch res; a gatekeeper has both branches and each needs a test. Auth is interestingly both — it decorates req.user on success — but having any reject branch makes it a gatekeeper for ordering purposes.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `pagingDefaults(req, res, next)` — middleware that NORMALIZES instead of rejecting: parse `req.query.page` / `req.query.perPage` (default 1 / 20, floor 1, perPage cap 100, non-numeric → default), write the resulting NUMBERS back onto `req.query.page` and `req.query.perPage`, call `next()`. Handlers downstream then use them without parsing.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: A decorator that moves the parsing gauntlet out of every list handler: downstream code reads `req.query.page` and gets a validated NUMBER. The cost is an implicit contract (handlers must know this ran) — which is why such middleware is mounted globally, making the contract universal.
hints: The familiar gauntlet, but the OUTPUT is written back onto req.query.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `normalizePath(req, res, next)`: rewrite `req.path` — lowercase it and strip ONE trailing slash unless the path is exactly `'/'` — then `next()`. `'/Users/42/'` → `'/users/42'`; `'/'` stays `'/'`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Mounted before the router, this makes `/Users/42/` and `/users/42` hit the same route — one middleware instead of normalization logic smeared across matchers. The `length > 1` guard protects the root path from becoming an empty string. (Real APIs often 301-redirect instead of silently rewriting; the normalize-early principle is the same.)
hints: Lowercase, then the conditional slice — guard the bare "/" case.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `denyPaths(blocked)` — factory over an array of exact paths. The middleware: `req.path` in the list → `403` with `{ error: { code: 'FORBIDDEN', message: 'access to <path> is blocked' } }`; otherwise `next()`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The same gatekeeper skeleton as blockMethods, keyed on path — proof that once you own the shape, new policies are parameter changes. Edge proxies run exactly such lists to keep internal endpoints (metrics, debug, admin) off the public internet even when the app ships them.
hints: Gatekeeper shape; includes over the closed-over list.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `composeMw(m1, m2)` returning a SINGLE middleware `(req, res, next)` that runs `m1`; if (and only if) m1 called its next, runs `m2`; if m2 also called its next, calls the OUTER `next()`. Short-circuits propagate: if either inner middleware responds without next, the composed middleware must not call the outer next.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Middleware form a monoid-ish algebra: two compose into one that behaves like both, so `composeMw(logger, composeMw(auth, guard))` flattens any stack into a single middleware. The elegant detail is handing m2 the outer `next` directly — no second flag needed, because m2 passing and the composition passing are the same event. runChain is this composition applied in a loop.
hints: Give m1 a private flag-next; only on the flag do you run m2.
m2 can receive the OUTER next directly — its pass IS the composition passing.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Build the engine. Export `runChain(middlewares, handler)` returning a composed handler `(req, res)` that:
1. Runs each middleware in array order, giving each a fresh `next` function.
2. If a middleware does NOT call its `next` (i.e. it responded — short-circuit), STOP: later middlewares and the handler must not run.
3. If all middlewares called next, run `handler(req, res)`.
An empty middleware array means the handler runs immediately.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: You just implemented the heart of Express (the real one adds async support and error routing, but this loop IS the idea). The fresh flag-plus-closure per middleware is the key move: `next` is not magic, just a callback whose invocation you observe. Test 4 shows why the same `req` object flows through everything — decorations made upstream are visible downstream because it is literally the same object.
hints: Loop the array; for each middleware create a flag and a next that sets it.
Flag not set after the call → return immediately.
The handler call goes AFTER the loop, so it only runs when the loop completes.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `makeRateLimiter(state, limit)` where `state` is a plain object used as a counter map. The middleware identifies the caller by the `x-client-id` header (lowercase key):
- no such header → `400` with `{ error: { code: 'BAD_REQUEST', message: 'x-client-id header required' } }`
- increment that client's count in `state` (first request = 1)
- if the count AFTER incrementing exceeds `limit`, respond `429` with `{ error: { code: 'RATE_LIMITED', message: 'too many requests' } }`
- otherwise `next()`.
So with limit 2, a client's 3rd request is rejected.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: A stateful gatekeeper: per-key counting (the `?? 0` idiom yet again) combined with the respond-or-next contract. Real limiters add time windows (counts reset every minute) and distributed storage, but the control flow — identify, count, compare, reject-or-pass — is exactly this. Note 429 still consumes a count: rejected requests are load too.
hints: The count-into-an-object pattern: `state[client] = (state[client] ?? 0) + 1`.
Three exits: 400 (unidentified), 429 (over limit), next() — in that order.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: The chain is `[requireRole('admin'), authenticate]` — guard first, auth second. What actually happens to an admin with a valid token?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Middleware run strictly in order and communicate only through `req`. The guard reads `req.user` before anything wrote it — undefined — and must reject (a guard that passes on missing users is a guard that fails open). Dependencies between middlewares ARE their order in the array.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Which pair of 401 messages is the best practice for (a) missing/malformed header and (b) well-formed but unknown token?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Two blandly distinct messages help honest clients (one says "you forgot the header", the other "re-login") without helping attackers (no echoed tokens, no usernames, no expiry intel, no hints about which tokens are close to valid). Option b echoes the attacker's own probe back with database context — never.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: A teammate suggests accepting tokens as `?token=abc123` "for easier testing". The main objection?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The Authorization header exists precisely because headers are NOT routinely logged, cached, bookmarked, or pasted into chat. URLs are. A token in the query string will end up in an access log within the hour and in a screenshot within the week. (This is the same reason the HTTP course had you scrub Authorization from logs.)

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The full authentication lookup in four lines: split the header, index into the token map, and an unknown token simply yields `undefined` — which the middleware converts into a 401. The map IS the session store; everything else is plumbing around this lookup.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `tokenOf(req)` returning the Bearer token from `req.headers.authorization`, or `null` when the header is missing, not `'Bearer <token>'` shaped (exactly two parts, scheme exactly `'Bearer'`), or the token is empty.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Deliberately strict and deliberately a pure function: the middleware that uses it stays four lines, and THIS part — the part attackers probe with malformed input — is testable with a plain object. Every `null` collapses into one 401 upstream.
hints: Same strict parse you wrote in the HTTP course, reading from req this time.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `makeAuth(usersByToken)` (a plain object mapping token → user object). The middleware:
- missing/malformed Authorization (not exactly `'Bearer <token>'`) → `401` with `{ error: { code: 'UNAUTHORIZED', message: 'authentication required' } }`
- well-formed but unknown token → `401` with `{ error: { code: 'UNAUTHORIZED', message: 'invalid token' } }`
- known token → set `req.user` to the user and call `next()`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The explanation's worked example, from your own hands. The design beats: injected token map (testable, swappable), strict parsing, two bland-but-distinct 401s, and the all-important decoration `req.user = user` — the single line the entire authorization story downstream depends on.
hints: Two failure tiers with two messages; success decorates req.user and passes on.
Parse strictly: exactly two parts, scheme exactly Bearer.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `requireRole(role)` — a factory returning middleware:
- `req.user` missing (no auth ran, or it failed open) → `401` with `{ error: { code: 'UNAUTHORIZED', message: 'authentication required' } }`
- `req.user.role !== role` → `403` with `{ error: { code: 'FORBIDDEN', message: 'requires role <role>' } }`
- matching role → `next()`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The 401-then-403 ladder encodes the distinction the HTTP course drilled: no identity → 401 (authenticate and retry makes sense); known identity, insufficient role → 403 (retrying changes nothing). The defensive 401 branch also makes the guard safe even when someone mounts it without auth — it fails CLOSED.
hints: Two guards in order: identity missing (401), then permission missing (403).
The factory makes `requireRole('admin')`, `requireRole('editor')` etc. from one definition.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `requireAnyRole(roles)` (an array) — like requireRole but passing when `req.user.role` is ANY of the listed roles. Missing user → `401` (same body as before); role not in the list → `403` with `{ error: { code: 'FORBIDDEN', message: 'requires one of: <roles joined by ", ">' } }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The generalization costs two tokens (`includes` for `===`) because the single-role version was already well-factored. Role lists appear the moment real orgs do ("admins OR moderators can delete comments") — and note `requireRole(r)` could now be defined as `requireAnyRole([r])`.
hints: Swap the equality for roles.includes; join the list into the message.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Strictly by the HTTP spec, a 401 response SHOULD also carry which header?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: 401 is formally a challenge: "authenticate like THIS and retry", with WWW-Authenticate naming the scheme. Browser Basic-auth popups are triggered by exactly this header. JSON APIs are often lax about it (clients know the scheme from the docs), but spec-complete APIs — and some strict clients — care.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `sessionToPublic(session)` — given `{ token, userId, role, expiresAt }`, return ONLY `{ userId, role, expiresAt }`. The token must never appear (this is what `GET /me/session` may show).
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The userToPublic discipline applied to auth data: an endpoint that shows "your session expires at..." must never echo the credential itself (the viewer already HAS it; a cross-site leak of the page must not). Allow-list serializers around every sensitive record, no exceptions for "internal" endpoints.
hints: Allow-list projection — three explicit reads.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `makeOptionalAuth(usersByToken)`: like makeAuth, but NEVER rejects. Valid known token → `req.user` = the user; anything else (missing header, malformed, unknown token) → `req.user = null`. ALWAYS calls `next()`. For endpoints that personalize when possible but work for everyone.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Same parsing, inverted policy: failure becomes `req.user = null` instead of a 401, and `next()` is unconditional. Setting the null default first means downstream code can rely on `req.user` EXISTING (as user-or-null) rather than sometimes-undefined — an explicit contract beats an implicit one. Public pages with a "logged in as..." corner run exactly this.
hints: Default req.user to null FIRST, then upgrade it if everything checks out.
There is no res call anywhere in this middleware.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Real tokens expire. Export `isExpired(session, now)` where `session` is `{ token, expiresAt }` (expiresAt: a timestamp number) and `now` is the current timestamp — `true` when `now` is at or past `expiresAt`. (The caller injects `now` — no `Date.now()` inside, which is what keeps this testable.)
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The comparison is trivial; the SIGNATURE is the lesson: by taking `now` as a parameter instead of calling `Date.now()`, the function is pure and the boundary case (`now === expiresAt`) is testable without clock mocking. Auth middleware would call it with the real clock: `if (isExpired(session, Date.now())) return unauthorized(res)` — the impurity stays at the edge.
hints: One comparison. The design content is in the signature.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `canAccess(user, ownerId)` → `true` when the user may touch a resource owned by `ownerId`: either `user.role === 'admin'` or `user.id === ownerId`. `user` may be `null` → `false`.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Admin-or-owner is the most common authorization rule in CRUD apps ("you can edit YOUR profile; admins can edit any"). Keeping it a pure predicate — no req, no res — means the same rule guards the API, filters lists, and decides whether the UI shows an Edit button.
hints: Null guard, then admin-or-owner in one || expression.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Which endpoint genuinely wants OPTIONAL auth (attach the user if possible, never reject)?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Public content with personalization sprinkled on top is the optional-auth habitat: anonymous visitors get the article, authenticated ones get it personalized. Anything that MUTATES or exposes private data wants mandatory auth — optional auth on a DELETE would mean "delete things, logged in or not".

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: A new `/reports` endpoint could be guarded with `requireAnyRole(['admin'])` or `requireAnyRole(['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'])` — nobody is sure who needs it yet. Which default is right, and why?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The failure modes are asymmetric: too-narrow produces a support ticket and a one-line PR; too-broad produces quiet data exposure you may never detect. Start closed, open on demand. (Option 3 — shipping unguarded "temporarily" — is how most real data leaks start.)

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Hierarchical roles become numbers so "at least editor" is a `>=`. The last line is the security-relevant one: an unknown role looks up `undefined`, and `undefined >= 1` is `false` — the comparison fails CLOSED. Accidental, but worth making deliberate with an explicit check, as the next exercise does.
hints: What does rank of an unknown role evaluate to, and how does >= treat it?

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `hasAtLeastRole(user, required)` with hierarchy viewer(1) < editor(2) < admin(3): `true` when the user's role ranks at or above the required role. `null` user, unknown user role, or unknown required role → `false`.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The output exercise showed unknown roles failing closed by accident of NaN-ish comparison; this version makes the policy explicit and readable. Hierarchies ('editor can do everything a viewer can') beat enumerating role lists on every route — `requireAnyRole(['admin','editor','viewer'])` becomes `atLeast('viewer')` — but only when the hierarchy is genuinely linear.
hints: A rank table plus explicit undefined checks for both lookups.
Unknown roles must fail closed — explicitly, not by luck.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `maskToken(token)` — keep the first 4 characters and replace the rest with `'***'`: `'t_abc123xyz'` → `'t_ab***'`. Tokens of length 4 or less → `'***'` entirely. Not a string → `'***'`.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: A 4-character prefix is enough to tell WHICH token appeared in a debug log ("was it the staging key or the prod key?") while being useless for replay. Masking short tokens entirely avoids the degenerate case where the prefix IS most of the secret. This belongs in any logging path that touches credentials.
hints: Type/length guard first, then slice(0, 4) + the mask.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Not everything is Bearer. Export `makeApiKeyAuth(validKeys)` (an array of accepted key strings). The middleware reads the `x-api-key` header (lowercase key):
- missing or not in the list → `401` `{ error: { code: 'UNAUTHORIZED', message: 'valid api key required' } }`
- valid → set `req.apiKey` to the key and call `next()`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: API keys are the machine-to-machine sibling of Bearer tokens: no user, no session — the KEY is the identity (of a client application), which is why the decoration is `req.apiKey` rather than `req.user`. Stripe, SendGrid, and most data APIs authenticate exactly this way. Note how little changed from makeAuth: header name, lookup, decoration. The shape is the knowledge.
hints: Same gatekeeper shape as makeAuth with a different header and lookup.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `requireVerified(req, res, next)` — roles are not the only gate. No `req.user` → `401` (standard body `{ error: { code: 'UNAUTHORIZED', message: 'authentication required' } }`); user present but `req.user.verified !== true` → `403` `{ error: { code: 'FORBIDDEN', message: 'email verification required' } }`; verified → `next()`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Authorization is any predicate over the authenticated identity: role, ownership, a verified flag, plan tier, feature flag. The strict `!== true` (rather than falsy-checking or `=== false`) means an absent field denies — new user objects are locked until something explicitly verifies them. Guards that fail closed survive schema drift; guards that fail open become incident reports.
hints: The 401/403 ladder again; the permission predicate is an attribute, not a role.
`!== true` makes a MISSING flag fail closed — test 3 checks exactly that.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `requireSelfOrAdmin(req, res, next)` guarding routes like `PATCH /users/:id`:
- no `req.user` → `401` `{ error: { code: 'UNAUTHORIZED', message: 'authentication required' } }`
- `req.user.role === 'admin'` → `next()` (admins touch anything)
- otherwise `req.user.id === req.params.id` → `next()`; else `403` `{ error: { code: 'FORBIDDEN', message: 'you may only modify your own account' } }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The canAccess predicate wearing its middleware uniform: identity from `req.user` (upstream auth), target from `req.params.id` (the router), decision by comparing the two. This is the guard whose ABSENCE is the #1 API vulnerability class (IDOR / broken object-level authorization): without it, any logged-in user can PATCH any `/users/:id` by changing the number.
hints: Three-rung ladder: 401 (no identity), pass (admin or owner), 403.
The owner check compares req.user.id to req.params.id — both strings.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Compose the whole stack WITHOUT runChain — by hand. Export `makeAdminOnlyDelete(usersByToken, store)`:
a single handler `(req, res)` for `DELETE /users/:id` that performs, in order:
1. Authentication (same rules/bodies as makeAuth: malformed → 401 'authentication required'; unknown token → 401 'invalid token').
2. Authorization: the authenticated user's role must be `'admin'` → else `403` `{ error: { code: 'FORBIDDEN', message: 'requires role admin' } }`.
3. The delete: `store.delete(req.params.id)` — deleted → `204` (no body); missing → `404` `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'user <id> not found' } }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Authenticate → authorize → act, flattened into one function so you can SEE the full gauntlet a protected request walks: 401, 401, 403, 404, then finally 204. Writing it inline once makes the middleware version (`runChain([auth, requireRole('admin')], removeHandler)`) feel earned rather than magical — it is this exact function, factored into reusable pieces. Note every rejecting branch leaves the store untouched: guards precede mutations, always.
hints: Four early-return gates: malformed auth, unknown token, wrong role, missing target — then the 204.
Every rejection must leave the store untouched; only the final gate mutates.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Routes registered in order: `/users/:id`, then `/users/new`. A request for `/users/new` arrives. What happens?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Simple routers (including Express) walk the table top-down and stop at the first match; `:id` happily captures the string 'new'. The rule of thumb: register literal routes before parameterized ones that could swallow them. (The handler then 404s looking up a user with id 'new' — a confusing bug to trace.)

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: What should `matchRoute('/health', '/health')` return, and why does it matter?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The return value carries two signals: matched-or-not, and the captures. `{}` vs `null` keeps them distinct — a route with no parameters still matches. Collapsing both into falsy values is how routers break on exactly the simplest routes.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The matching loop over pre-split segments: literals must equal, `:`-segments capture. Here everything lines up — matched is true, `:id` captured `'42'`, and exactly one capture exists. Change `'posts'` to `'comments'` in either array and matched flips to false.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `isParamSegment(segment)` → `true` when the segment starts with `':'` (like `':id'`), else `false`.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Trivial alone, but naming the predicate pays in the matcher: `if (isParamSegment(ps[i]))` reads as the rule it implements. Tiny named predicates are how non-trivial algorithms stay legible.
hints: One startsWith call.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `segmentsOf(pathOrPattern)` splitting on `'/'` and dropping empty strings: `'/users/:id/'` → `['users', ':id']`; `'/'` → `[]`.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Filtering empties makes the matcher immune to trailing-slash differences for free: `/users/` and `/users` produce identical segment arrays, so they match the same routes. One normalization, placed early, deletes a whole category of 404 bug reports.
hints: split + filter — leading AND trailing slashes produce empties.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `matchRoute(pattern, path)`:
- Split both into non-empty segments; different lengths → `null`.
- Walk the segments: a pattern segment starting with `':'` captures the path segment under its name (without the colon); any other segment must be equal, else `null`.
- Matched → return the params object (`{}` when the pattern had no captures).
`matchRoute('/users/:id', '/users/42')` → `{ id: '42' }`; `matchRoute('/health', '/health')` → `{}`; `matchRoute('/users/:id', '/posts/42')` → `null`.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The core algorithm of every router you have ever used, in a dozen lines: length gate, then capture-or-compare per segment. The two-signal return (object = matched + captures, null = no) is the function's real design content. Express compiles patterns to regexes for speed, but the SEMANTICS are exactly these segments.
hints: Length check first — it rules out most non-matches instantly.
Inside the loop: capture or compare, nothing else.
Return the object even when empty; null ONLY for a failed match.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `pathFor(pattern, params)` substituting params INTO a pattern: `pathFor('/users/:id/posts/:postId', { id: '4', postId: '9' })` → `'/users/4/posts/9'`. A parameter missing from `params` → return `null`. Extra params are ignored.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: matchRoute run backwards: patterns are a two-way street (parse paths in, generate links out), and client code uses exactly this to build URLs without string concatenation typos. Failing hard (null) on a missing param beats emitting `/users/undefined` — a string you WILL otherwise meet in production logs.
hints: Walk the pattern segments, substituting the : ones from params.
A missing param is a hard null — half-built paths are worse than none.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Routers get mounted under prefixes (all API routes under `/api`). Export `stripPrefix(prefix, path)`: when `path` starts with the prefix at a segment boundary, return the rest (at least `'/'`); otherwise `null`. `stripPrefix('/api', '/api/users')` → `'/users'`; `stripPrefix('/api', '/api')` → `'/'`; `stripPrefix('/api', '/apiary')` → `null`.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The `'/apiary'` case is the teeth: naive `startsWith('/api')` matches it, leaking unrelated routes into your API router. Requiring the prefix to end at a segment boundary (`prefix + '/'` or exact match) is the correct rule — the same one Express applies when you `app.use('/api', router)`.
hints: Two positive cases: exact equality, or startsWith(prefix + '/').
The '/apiary' trap is why you must NOT just use startsWith(prefix).

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `routeDecision(routes, method, path)` where `routes` is an array of `{ method, pattern }` (no handlers — just the table). Walk IN ORDER:
- First route whose method AND pattern match → `{ index, params }` (its array index and the captures).
- Otherwise, if some route's PATTERN matches but with a different method → `{ status: 405 }` (the path exists, the verb is wrong).
- Nothing matches at all → `{ status: 404 }`.
Use matchRoute's rules for patterns (you may re-implement it internally).
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The 404/405 distinction requires remembering partial evidence: a pattern that matched under the wrong method proves the PATH exists, so if the walk ends without a full match, 405 beats 404. One boolean carries that memory through the loop. APIs that always 404 instead are merely less helpful — this is the polish difference.
hints: Track a boolean: did ANY pattern match the path (regardless of method)?
Full match → return immediately (first match wins). Pattern-only match → remember and keep looking.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Three behaviors of the matcher on display: multi-param capture (4 and 9), the length-mismatch null (true), and the matched-but-empty `{}` — which stringifies to `{}`, visibly distinct from null. Keep that last distinction sacred when you implement it yourself.
hints: Two captures, one length mismatch, one match-with-no-captures.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `countParams(pattern)` — how many `:param` segments the pattern has: `'/posts/:postId/comments/:id'` → 2, `'/health'` → 0.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: A one-line metric with a design use: route tables where some pattern has 4+ captures are usually over-nested (remember the deep-nesting quiz from the REST course). Counting captures per route is a lint for URL design.
hints: Filter the :segments, take the length.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `paramNames(pattern)` returning the parameter names in order: `'/posts/:postId/comments/:id'` → `['postId', 'id']`; a pattern with none → `[]`.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: A split-filter-map pipeline answering "what will this route capture?" — useful for documentation generators and for validating that `pathFor` received every needed param before dispatch. (Empty segments need no special handling here: `''` does not start with `':'`.)
hints: split → filter the :segments → map off the colon.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `isStaticPattern(pattern)` → `true` when the pattern captures nothing (no `':'` segments): `'/users/new'` → `true`, `'/users/:id'` → `false`.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The predicate behind the route-ordering rule: static patterns should be registered (or sorted) before parameterized ones so `/users/new` is not swallowed by `/users/:id`. The next exercise turns that rule into code.
hints: No segment starts with a colon — some() negated.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `sortRoutesStaticFirst(patterns)` — given an array of pattern strings, return a NEW array with all static patterns (no ':' segments) first, then the parameterized ones, preserving the original relative order within each group (a stable partition). Do not mutate the input.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Two filter passes spliced together guarantee stability trivially (each group keeps its internal order), which `.sort` only promises if you trust the engine's stability and write the comparator carefully. Run your route table through this before building the router and the `/users/new`-shadowing class of bug is structurally gone.
hints: Two filters concatenated IS a stable partition — simpler than sort with a comparator.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `patternsOverlap(a, b)` → `true` when some concrete path could match BOTH patterns: same non-empty-segment count, and at every position the segments are compatible (equal literals, or at least one of the two is a `:param`).
`('/users/:id', '/users/new')` → `true` (the path '/users/new' matches both); `('/users/:id', '/posts/:id')` → `false`; different lengths → `false`.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: A static analysis over your route table: two overlapping patterns mean registration order silently decides winners — sometimes intended (`/users/new` before `/users/:id`), sometimes a bug (two teams both claiming `/items/:id`). Running this across all pattern pairs at startup and warning on unexpected overlaps is cheap insurance frameworks like Fastify actually implement.
hints: Mirror matchRoute, but comparing pattern to PATTERN.
A position only disqualifies when BOTH sides are literals and they differ.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Our router checks routes one by one — O(n) per request. When does this actually matter, and what do big frameworks do?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Linear scan over 40 routes is nanoseconds next to one database query — optimize it never. At hundreds of routes (large APIs, API gateways), radix/prefix trees walk the path segment by segment, eliminating whole subtrees per step; that is what Fastify's find-my-way does. Knowing WHERE the naive version stops being fine is the actual engineering skill.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: A request URL is `/users/42?fields=name`. What must happen before `matchRoute` sees it?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Routing and query parsing are separate stages on separate components of the URL: the path picks the handler, the query parameterizes it. Feeding the raw URL to the matcher would make `'42?fields=name'` the captured id — a bug you can now spot on sight.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `buildRouter(routes)` where routes is an array of `{ method, pattern, handler }`. Return a single dispatcher handler `(req, res)` that:
1. Walks the table in order; the first route where `route.method === req.method` AND the pattern matches `req.path` wins.
2. Sets `req.params` to the captured params, then calls `route.handler(req, res)`.
3. No match → `404` with `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'no route for <METHOD> <path>' } }`.
(Matching rules as in matchRoute; implement it internally or inline.)

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: buildRouter + matchRoute + runChain is a working web framework core — you have now written all three. The dispatcher is just linear search with first-match-wins (test 3 proves the ordering rule from the quiz), and setting `req.params` before the handler call is the hand-off that makes every params exercise from earlier lessons work. The post-loop 404 speaks the standard envelope, so even "no route" looks like every other error.
hints: Method gate first (cheap), pattern match second.
On a hit: assign req.params, call the handler, RETURN.
The 404 sits after the loop — it runs only when nothing claimed the request.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Real route tables attach middleware per route. Export `buildRouterWithMiddleware(routes)` where each route is `{ method, pattern, middlewares, handler }` (middlewares: possibly-empty array of `(req, res, next)`). Dispatch as in buildRouter, but on a match run the route's middlewares in order first — a middleware that does not call `next` short-circuits (the handler must not run). No route matched → the same 404 envelope as buildRouter.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The two engines you built, fused: dispatch finds the route, then the chain loop runs its guards, then the handler. The ordering subtlety test 3 pins down — params must be set before middleware run — is exactly what lets an ownership guard compare `req.user.id` to `req.params.id`. This is, at honest scale, how `app.get('/users/:id', auth, guard, handler)` works.
hints: buildRouter + the runChain loop, inlined at the match site.
Set req.params BEFORE the middlewares — guards like requireSelfOrAdmin read them.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: For `GET /todos?q=ship&sort=title&page=2`, why must sorting happen BEFORE pagination?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: "Page 2 sorted by title" means: sort everything, THEN take the second window. Slice-then-sort gives you a tidy-looking page of the wrong items — a bug users report as "my item disappears when I sort". Filter→sort→paginate mirrors SQL's WHERE → ORDER BY → LIMIT for the same reason.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Your list handler does `todos.sort((a, b) => ...)` directly on the injected store array. What goes wrong?
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Array.prototype.sort mutates its receiver (one of the classic JS surprises). A GET handler that reorders the shared store violates the safe-method promise from the HTTP course — reads must not write. The fix is one spread: `[...todos].sort(...)` sorts a copy.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: In the finished /todos API, where does each concern live? Pick the correct mapping.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The layering is the course: each concern sits where it is most testable and most reusable. The handler ends up as a thin translator — orchestrating pure pieces and speaking HTTP — which is why the capstones read as composition rather than fresh logic. When a new endpoint fits this map without debate, the architecture is doing its job.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `filterTodos(todos, query)` (query: raw strings object):
- `query.done` is `'true'` or `'false'` → keep todos whose `done` matches (other values of done: ignore the filter)
- `query.q` is a non-empty string → keep todos whose `title` contains it case-insensitively
- both filters can combine; no filters → all todos (same order). Return a new array; never mutate.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: Composable filtering: each optional stage narrows `result`, and stages stack naturally (the combined case applies both). Returning a copy even when nothing filtered keeps the contract uniform — callers may mutate the result (sort it!) without touching the store. This is the WHERE clause of your API.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Export `sortTodos(todos, sortValue)` — sortValue like `'title'`, `'-priority'`, or absent:
- `null`/`undefined`/`''` → return a COPY in the original order
- field `'title'` (strings: compare with `<`/`>`) or `'priority'` / `'id'` (numbers) — `'-'` prefix means descending
- unknown field → copy in original order.
Never mutate the input.
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: All the sort hygiene in one place: copy before sorting (the mutation quiz made the case), whitelist the sortable fields (an unknown field must not crash — and remember the injection quiz: this value came off the URL), and the `-` prefix flips the comparator's sign rather than reversing afterwards (reversal would also flip the order of EQUAL elements — a subtle stability bug).

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
Assemble the read side. Export `makeListTodos(todos)` (array store). The handler processes `req.query`:
1. Filter: `done` (`'true'`/`'false'`, else ignored), `q` (non-empty → case-insensitive title substring).
2. Sort: `sort` value with fields `title`/`priority`/`id`, `'-'` prefix descending; absent/unknown → original order. NEVER mutate the store.
3. Paginate: `page` (default 1, floor 1), `perPage` (default 20, floor 1, cap 100), non-numeric → defaults.
Respond `200` with `{ data, meta: { page, perPage, total, totalPages } }` where `total` counts the FILTERED set.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The flagship read endpoint, whole: hostile query inputs tamed stage by stage, the store protected from mutation, meta measured at the right point (after filter, before slice). Every real list endpoint — products, orders, posts — is this handler with different field names. If you can write this from a blank starter, the read half of REST is yours.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
The write side. Export `makeCreateTodo(todos)` (array store). Validate `req.body` accumulating ALL errors (strings, in this order):
- `title`: required non-empty string, max 100 chars → `'title is required'` / `'title must be a string'` / `'title must be at most 100 characters'` (empty string counts as required-missing)
- `priority`: optional; when present must be an integer 1-5 → `'priority must be an integer between 1 and 5'`
Errors → `400` with `{ error: { code: 'VALIDATION', message: 'validation failed', details: errors } }`, store untouched.
Valid → push `{ id, title, done: false, priority }` (id = numeric max of existing ids + 1, or 1; priority defaults to 3) and respond `201` with `{ data: todo }`. Treat a null/undefined body as `{}`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The full write choreography with every convention this course taught: errors accumulated (not first-only), the details array riding inside the standard envelope, the store untouched on any failure, defaults applied when building the stored object (never trusted from the client — `done` is ALWAYS false on create), and the 201 receipt showing the stored truth. - `priority` (optional): `'priority must be an integer between 1 and 5'`

Export `applyListQuery(todos, query)` composing filter and sort (no pagination) as pure data flow:

- then sort by `query.sort` (fields title/priority/id, '-' prefix desc, absent/unknown → keep order)
Return a new array; never mutate.

With this extracted, `makeListTodos` becomes parse-paginate-respond around one call — and the pipeline itself is testable with table-driven cases like these, no recorder in sight. bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions: Export `todoStats(todos)` returning `{ total, done, open, pctDone }` — counts plus the percentage of done todos, rounded with `Math.round` (0 for an empty list). `[done, open, open]`-ish input → `{ total: 3, done: 1, open: 2, pctDone: 33 }`.

bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.instructions:
The final assembly. Export `makeTodosApi(todos, usersByToken)` returning `{ list, create }` where BOTH handlers require authentication, and creation additionally requires a role.

Auth (both handlers, first): Authorization must be exactly `'Bearer <token>'` with a token in `usersByToken` → else `401` `{ error: { code: 'UNAUTHORIZED', message: 'authentication required' } }` (one message for all auth failures here).

`list`: after auth, respond `200` with `{ data }` — the todos filtered to `done: false` ONLY when `req.query.open` is `'true'`, else all todos. (No pagination here.)

`create`: after auth, the user's `role` must be `'editor'` or `'admin'` → else `403` `{ error: { code: 'FORBIDDEN', message: 'requires one of: editor, admin' } }`. Then `title` must be a non-empty string → else `400` `{ error: { code: 'VALIDATION', message: 'title is required' } }`. Then push `{ id: max+1 (or 1), title, done: false, priority: 3, createdBy: user.id }` and respond `201` `{ data: todo }`.

*(Simulation convention: `req` is a plain object; `res` is the usual recorder — `statusCode` default 200, `body` default undefined, chainable `status(code)` / `json(body)`. A middleware is `(req, res, next)`: it either calls `next()` exactly once to pass control on, or responds via `res` and does NOT call `next`.)*
bootforge/express-api/middleware-and-rou.explanation: The whole course in one factory: shared auth as a private closure helper, the 401→403→400→201 gauntlet in canonical order (identity before permission before validity — each check meaningless without the previous), the viewer/editor split showing role granularity, and `createdBy` sourced from the authenticated identity rather than the body (clients do not get to claim authorship). You have now built every layer of a backend web API as pure, tested functions — Express will feel like familiar furniture when you meet the real thing.
hints: Write authenticate(req) → user-or-null ONCE inside the factory; both handlers call it.
Gauntlet order in create: 401 → 403 → 400 → mutate → 201.
createdBy comes from the TOKEN (req.user equivalent), never from the body.
